name: constexpr-sql
listed_description: A compile-time SQL query parser and executor in C++17.
reason: Benchmark exists but its baseline is not a recognizable incumbent. README 'Correctness and Performance Testing' says SQLite3 is used only to check correctness of 1.5 million generated queries; the performance pipeline (tests/perf/scripts/runner.py, g++ -std=c++2a -O3, /usr/bin/time user seconds, 65 thousand iterations, 256 for CROSS JOIN) compares six queries against the author's own hand-coded C++ loops with std::vector and std::unordered_map. Checked-in results in tests/perf/data (user seconds, hand-coded then library): query0 6.39 vs 6.81, query1 4.18 vs 4.73, query2 11.17 vs 3.70, query3 12.39 vs 11.81, query4 3.45 vs 1.54, query5 44.35 vs 38.04; no CPU model, no SQLite timing, and the presentation PDF has no numbers. Open issues cover only compile failures. No numeric comparison against SQLite or any other named baseline exists.

name: EJDB2
reason: No numeric comparison anywhere reachable. The README (JQL, indexes, performance tips only about its own index versus scan choice) and the repo front page contain no benchmark or comparison with SQLite, MongoDB or LMDB; web search found only db-engines.com feature comparison pages. Lead: its storage layer IOWOW/IWKV (github.com/Softmotions/iowow) claims 'good performance comparing its main competitors: lmdb, leveldb, kyoto cabinet' in its README with no numbers there, and an ioarena fork is mentioned in search snippets; IOWOW is a separate project not in the catalog.

name: Groonga
reason: Directional claims only, no numbers in reachable sources. README is a link page; doc/source/characteristic.rst says 'fast and accurate full text search engine' and that column stores suit aggregate queries better than MySQL and PostgreSQL, with no figures. The benchmark/ directory holds internal microbenchmarks (bench-cache.c, bench-geo-select.c, bench-range-select.c, others) with no external baseline. Search snippets mention a 2011 '100x faster than Sphinx' slide, Mroonga being faster than MyISAM/InnoDB full text, and PGroonga index build 25m37s vs pg_bigm 5h56m15s; those are separate projects or blocked or snippet-only pages, none a Groonga-versus-SQLite/BerkeleyDB number. groonga.org docs are blocked in this environment.

name: hiberlite
reason: No numeric comparison anywhere reachable. README (722 stars, BSD-3-Clause, 59 commits) has no benchmark, overhead figure or comparison with raw sqlite3 or other ORMs; repo files are sample.cpp, tests.cpp, catch_tests.cpp only. A web search for C++ SQLite ORM benchmarks found only ODB's own results (7ms per 500 iterations on SQLite 3.7.5) and no table that includes hiberlite.

name: Hiredis
reason: No numeric comparison of hiredis against a named baseline. README has no benchmark or performance comparison (it only mentions buffer-size tuning); the repo has no benchmark directory. Web results are about other things: a gist benchmarking the Node.js hiredis parser against a JavaScript parser (hiredis was the slower one at 44543 vs 46189 ops/sec for PING at 200 clients, Core 2 Duo Mac mini), snippets on the hiredis-py Python parser (a binding of this library, a wrapper) being up to 10x faster in parsing, and a snippet of C with hiredis at 340,000 commands/s vs Ruby redis-rb 150,000 whose source page was not opened. Hiredis is the reference client rather than a challenger, so no baseline it beats was found.
